blog.title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages

pageTitle: The chat history that kept growing
summary: Discord says its messages outgrew MongoDB around 100 million. This story follows why it chose Cassandra, then the problems it reports: oversized partitions, edit and delete races, tombstones, and a six-month surprise.

hook.teaser: A chat app promises to keep every message forever. What happens when the pile outgrows the first database?

media.alt: A tall pile of chat bubbles drops onto a small whiteboard that is already full. A worried desk worker looks up at it.
A ring of desks, each with a notebook, a whiteboard and a folder. A new bubble lands on one desk while a worker nearby waves.

blocks.deck: Discord decided to keep every message forever. What does it take to store that pile, and what went wrong on the way?

blocks.kicker: Distributed systems / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: From one database to a ring of desks

chapters.title: The whiteboard filled up
chapters.caption: Discord started on MongoDB, one database for everything. Around November 2015 it reached 100 million stored messages. The team says the data and the index could no longer fit in RAM, and speed became unpredictable. Think of a whiteboard that is too small for the notes.

media.alt: A small whiteboard crammed with notes, some falling off the edge. A worker holds a stack of extra notes and frowns.

chapters.title: Pick a database that grows by adding desks
chapters.caption: Discord wrote down what it needed: grow without reshuffling data by hand, heal itself, need little upkeep, and give steady speed. The post says Cassandra was the only database that met all of its requirements.

media.alt: A checklist pinned to a wall with ticks for growing, healing, low upkeep and steady speed. A ring of desks sits beside it.

chapters.title: Cut the folders into ten-day slices
chapters.caption: Each channel's messages first lived in one big folder, and folders grew past 100MB. Discord says that put heavy pressure on Cassandra and kept data from spreading around. So it started a new folder for about 10 days of messages. It also later learned some rough edges: edits and deletes can collide, and deletes leave markers called tombstones.

media.alt: One long folder is cut into several short folders, each labeled with a calendar strip. A worker points at the newest one.

chapters.title: What Discord reports
chapters.caption: Discord reports writes under 1 millisecond and reads under 5 milliseconds in a week of testing. It also reports a surprise six months after launch: one channel with millions of deleted messages made Cassandra stall. These are the company's own numbers, not an outside test. See The Big Surprise in the post ↗

media.alt: A stopwatch showing a quick tick beside a worry meter that swings high. A stack of delete markers sits on a desk.

blocks.title: What Discord ran into
blocks.deck: Read each strip from left to right. This is one team's account of its own move, in its own words.
blocks.howTo: The drawings are made up to explain the idea. The names under “grown-up words” are the usual names for them. Discord's numbers are in the evidence box at the end, and they are company-reported.

panels.caption: Discord's first version stored everything in MongoDB. That was good for building fast.

media.alt: A single whiteboard on a wall with a few neat notes. A worker smiles and sticks one more on.

panels.caption: By about 100 million messages, the team says the data and the index no longer fit in RAM.

media.alt: A whiteboard covered edge to edge with notes. A worker holds one more note with nowhere to put it.

panels.caption: Speed became unpredictable. Discord decided it was time to move to a database that suited the job.

media.alt: A worry meter swings between low and high. A worker shrugs at a packing box labeled new database.

strips.title: What the new database must do
strips.grownUpWords: linear scalability, automatic failover, predictable performance

panels.caption: Discord wrote a list. First: grow by adding machines, with no hand-moving of data.

media.alt: A ring of desks with one new desk being wheeled in. Arrows show the ring stretching to include it.

panels.caption: Next: heal itself, need little upkeep, and keep a steady response time without a helper cache.

media.alt: One desk goes dark and its neighbors cover for it. A worker sleeps in a chair, happy.

panels.caption: Discord says Cassandra was the only database that met every item on its list.

media.alt: A checklist with every box ticked and a ring of desks stamped with a green tick.

panels.caption: In Cassandra, a channel's messages sit together in one folder, called a partition.

media.alt: A desk with one folder labeled with a channel name, stuffed with message slips.

panels.caption: Discord saw warnings about folders over 100MB. A channel can grow for years, and a big folder cannot be spread around the ring.

media.alt: A very fat folder that will not fit through a door to the next desk. A worker pulls at it.

panels.caption: The fix: a new folder about every 10 days. Finding recent messages means opening the newest folders first.

media.alt: Several slim folders on a shelf, each with a calendar tab. A worker reaches for the newest one.

strips.title: An edit meets a delete
strips.grownUpWords: upsert, last write wins, eventual consistency

panels.caption: One person edits a message. At the same moment, another person deletes it.

media.alt: Two workers at two desks reach for the same message slip. One holds a pen, one holds scissors.

panels.caption: Cassandra treats every write as a small update of one column. So the row was left with only a few pieces and the rest missing.

media.alt: A message slip with most of it blank. Only the name tab and a few words remain.

panels.caption: Discord's fix: treat a row missing its required author as broken, and delete it.

media.alt: A worker spots a half-empty slip, shakes his head and drops it in a bin.

panels.caption: In Cassandra a delete does not erase at once. It leaves a small marker, a tombstone, so other machines hear about it.

media.alt: A worker puts a tiny cross-marked flag on a message slip instead of tearing it up.

panels.caption: Writing an empty value leaves the same marker. Discord's message form has 16 boxes, and the average message fills only 4.

media.alt: A form with sixteen boxes. Four are filled, twelve are blank with tiny flags on them.

panels.caption: So most of the time Discord was leaving 12 markers for no reason. The fix was simple: write only the boxes that have a value.

media.alt: A worker fills in only four boxes and leaves the rest bare, with no flags. A tidy desk.

panels.caption: Six months after the switch, Cassandra went unresponsive. It kept pausing for about 10 seconds at a time while cleaning up memory.

media.alt: A desk worker frozen mid-step with a big clock beside him and a heap of paper scraps piling up.

panels.caption: The cause: a channel where millions of messages had been deleted, leaving one. Loading it meant wading through millions of markers.

media.alt: A huge heap of tiny flags with one lonely message slip at the bottom. A worker digs through the heap.

panels.caption: Discord shortened how long markers live, from 10 days to 2 days, and tracked empty folders so it skips them.

media.alt: A worker with a stamp marking an empty folder skip. A shorter calendar strip sits beside a smaller heap.
